title: Which Summary to Quote, and What the Units Are
unit: Mean, Median, Mode and Standard Deviation
quickIdea: Mean for symmetric data, median when there are outliers or open-ended classes, mode for categories; and of the four summaries only the standard deviation carries the data's units.
remember: Symmetric data without outliers: the mean, because it uses every value and adds up correctly across groups.
Skewed data, or data with outliers or open-ended classes ('1000 and above'): the median, because it cannot be dragged and needs no midpoint.
Categories with no order: the mode, and nothing else - a mean of colours is not a number with a meaning.
Variance is in squared units, the standard deviation is in the data's units, and the coefficient of variation sd/mean is unitless, which is what makes it the right comparison across different scales.
The coefficient of variation is defined only for a positive mean, so it is meaningless for data centred on zero.

The empirical rule - about 68 percent within one standard deviation, 95 within two, 99.7 within three - is a statement about roughly normal data. Applying it to a skewed set is a category error, not a rounding error.
In an exam, 'average' means the mean unless the data is described as skewed, and 'spread' means the standard deviation unless the variance is named explicitly.

example.prompt: Two machines produce parts with mean length 100 mm. Machine A has standard deviation 5 mm and machine B has standard deviation 20 mm. Compare their relative variability.
example.work: CV(A) = 5/100 = 0.05, or 5 percent. CV(B) = 20/100 = 0.20, or 20 percent. The ratio of the standard deviations is 4, and the ratio of the coefficients of variation is also 4 because the means are equal.
example.answer: Machine B is four times as variable relative to its mean; the coefficients of variation are 5 percent and 20 percent.

gateAngle: The choice of summary is the first step of every question in this topic and is never tested on its own. Where GATE does test it, it does so inside a skewness or an invariance question, which is why those cards carry the PYQs and this one does not.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A grouped table of salaries has a final open class of '200000 and above'. Which of the mean, median and mode can be computed, and which cannot?
variations.answer: The median and the mode can; the mean cannot be computed exactly.
variations.why: The mean needs a midpoint for every class, and an open class has none. The median needs only the cumulative frequencies and the boundaries, and the mode needs only the frequencies.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A data set has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is its coefficient of variation, and what does the number mean?
variations.why: CV = sd/mean = 10/50 = 0.2. It says the typical distance from the mean is a fifth of the mean, which is a scale-free statement and can be compared with a data set measured in different units.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A data set is strongly right-skewed with mean 80 and standard deviation 40. A candidate claims about 68 percent of the values lie between 40 and 120. What is wrong?
variations.answer: The empirical rule applies to roughly normal data, not to a skewed set.
variations.why: With a strong right tail the mass between mean minus one standard deviation and mean plus one standard deviation need not be near 68 percent. The rule is a property of the normal family, and the question has told you the data is not in it.

trap.what: Comparing variances of data sets measured in different units, or applying the empirical rule to a skewed set.
trap.why: A variance carries squared units, so two variances are comparable only when the units and the scales match. And the 68/95/99.7 percentages are a property of the normal distribution, not of standard deviations in general.
trap.counterexample: A variance of 4 in centimetres squared and a variance of 4 in metres squared describe spreads that differ by a factor of 10000. Comparing them directly says the two data sets are equally variable, which is false.

check.question: A data set has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is its coefficient of variation?
check.explanation: CV = standard deviation / mean = 10/50 = 0.2. It is unitless, so it can be compared with the coefficient of variation of a data set in other units.
